Optimal dose finding with the BOIN-ET family

Source: vignettes/simFastBOIN-boin-et.Rmd
simFastBOIN-boin-et.Rmd

Why the optimal biological dose

For chemotherapy the most effective dose is usually taken to be the most toxic one that is still acceptable, the maximum tolerated dose (MTD). For targeted and immune therapies the response may level off, or even fall, below the MTD, and the aim is then the optimal biological dose (OBD), which weighs the response against the toxicity. The BOIN-ET design of Takeda, Taguri and Morita (2018) decides the next dose from both the DLT rate and the response rate at the current dose, and selects the OBD at the end of the trial.

The package provides six designs of this family:

  • BOIN-ET (Takeda et al., 2018), in which every cohort is assessed before the next one is dosed: sim_boin_et() and sim_boin_et_multi();
  • TITE-BOIN-ET (Takeda, Morita and Taguri, 2020), which doses new patients while earlier ones are still assessed: sim_tite_boin_et() and sim_tite_boin_et_multi();
  • BF-BOIN-ET (Takeda, Zhu and Hirakawa, 2025), which treats at lower doses the patients who arrive while a cohort is assessed: sim_bf_boin_et() and sim_bf_boin_et_multi();
  • BOIN-ETC (Kakizume, Takeda, Taguri and Morita, 2024), for two drugs given together, which runs BOIN-ET in subtrials of the dose matrix: sim_boin_etc() and sim_boin_etc_multi();
  • gBOIN-ET (Takeda, Morita and Taguri, 2022), for toxicity and efficacy outcomes graded in categories that carry scores: sim_gboin_et() and sim_gboin_et_multi();
  • TITE-gBOIN-ET (Takeda, Yamaguchi, Taguri and Morita, 2023), its time-to-event version: sim_tite_gboin_et() and sim_tite_gboin_et_multi().

The rules follow the R packages of the authors, ‘boinet’ (Yamaguchi, Takeda and Maruo, 2025) for BOIN-ET, TITE-BOIN-ET, gBOIN-ET and TITE-gBOIN-ET and ‘bfboinet’ for BF-BOIN-ET, with the changes described below, and the article for BOIN-ETC, with the rules of the code of the authors as options. The trials and the selection of the OBD run in C++.

The boundaries and the decision table

The DLT rate at the current dose is compared with two boundaries, lambda1 and lambda2, and the response rate with one, eta1. They minimize the probability of an incorrect decision, as found by the grid search of boinet::gridoptim().

bd <- boin_et_boundary(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60)
bd
#> BOIN-ET boundaries
#>   target DLT rate      : 0.3
#>   target response rate : 0.6
#>   p_saf / p_tox        : 0.03 / 0.42
#>   p_saf_resp           : 0.36
#> 
#>   lambda1 (escalate)   : 0.14
#>   lambda2 (de-escalate): 0.35
#>   eta1 (response)      : 0.48
#>   probability of an incorrect decision: 0.04703

With a target DLT rate of 0.30, a target response rate of 0.60 and the design parameters of Takeda et al. (2018), the boundaries are 0.14 for lambda1, 0.35 for lambda2 and 0.48 for eta1, the values of the article. The decision at the current dose is then

  • E, escalate, when the DLT rate is at most lambda1 and the response rate at most eta1;
  • S, stay, when the DLT rate is below lambda2 and the response rate above eta1;
  • D, de-escalate, when the DLT rate is at least lambda2;
  • E/S/D otherwise, which moves to the dose with the highest observed response rate among the current dose and its neighbors, or escalates when the next higher dose has not been tried.
boin_et_decision_table(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, n = c(3, 6))
#> BOIN-ET decision table
#>   lambda1 = 0.14, lambda2 = 0.35, eta1 = 0.48
#> 
#> 3 patients
#>     Responses
#> DLTs 0     1     2  3 
#>    0 E     E     S  S 
#>    1 E/S/D E/S/D S  S 
#>    2 D     D     D  D 
#>    3 D*    D*    D* D*
#> 
#> 6 patients
#>     Responses
#> DLTs 0     1     2     3  4  5  6 
#>    0 E     E     E     S  S  S  S 
#>    1 E/S/D E/S/D E/S/D S  S  S  S 
#>    2 E/S/D E/S/D E/S/D S  S  S  S 
#>    3 D     D     D     D  D  D  D 
#>    4 D*    D*    D*    D* D* D* D*
#>    5 D*    D*    D*    D* D* D* D*
#>    6 D*    D*    D*    D* D* D* D*
#> 
#> E = escalate, S = stay, D = de-escalate, E/S/D = choose among the current and neighboring doses;
#> * = the dose is no longer admissible

These are the decisions of Table 2 of Takeda et al. (2018). A star marks the counts that make a dose inadmissible: by default, as in ‘boinet’, a dose is excluded when the posterior probability that its DLT rate exceeds target is above cutoff_eli = 0.95, or when the posterior probability that its response rate is below p_saf_resp is above cutoff_eli_resp = 0.99. p_eli and p_eli_resp change the two rates; the simulations of the article exclude a dose when the posterior probability that its DLT rate is below 0.40 is less than 0.10, or that its response rate is above 0.20 is less than 0.10 (p_eli = 0.40, p_eli_resp = 0.20, cutoff_eli = 0.90 and cutoff_eli_resp = 0.90).

Operating characteristics for one scenario

Scenario 1 of Takeda et al. (2018) has six doses, twelve cohorts of three patients and a trial that starts at the lowest dose.

p_true <- c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40)
p_resp <- c(0.05, 0.35, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.70)

oc <- sim_boin_et(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true,
                  p_resp = p_resp, n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3,
                  n_trials = 2000, seed = 123)
oc
#> BOIN-ET operating characteristics
#>   target DLT rate      : 0.3
#>   target response rate : 0.6
#>   trials               : 2000
#>   cohorts              : 12 of size 3
#>   max sample size      : 36
#>   lambda1 / lambda2    : 0.14 / 0.35
#>   eta1                 : 0.48
#>   OBD selection        : max_resp with observed response rates
#> 
#>                        DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5  DL6 Total / No OBD
#> True DLT rate (%)      5.0 15.0 25.0 30.0 35.0 40.0               
#> True response rate (%) 5.0 35.0 55.0 65.0 75.0 70.0               
#> OBD selected (%)       1.5 16.1 47.1 26.7  7.0  0.5            1.1
#> Patients treated       3.5  8.9 14.3  7.1  1.8  0.2           35.8
#> Patients with DLT      0.2  1.3  3.6  2.2  0.6  0.1            8.0
#> Patients with response 0.2  3.1  7.9  4.7  1.4  0.1           17.3
#> 
#> Trials stopped early: 1.1%

The output gives the percentage of trials selecting each dose as the OBD, the average numbers of patients, DLTs and responses at each dose, and the percentage of trials stopped early. Here dose 3 is selected most often, in 47 percent of the trials, and 1.1 percent of the trials select no OBD.

Several scenarios are run with sim_boin_et_multi(). In scenario 7 of the article the response rate peaks at dose 2 while the DLT rate goes on rising.

scenarios <- list(
  list(name = "Scenario 1", p_true = p_true, p_resp = p_resp),
  list(name = "Scenario 7", p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.55),
       p_resp = c(0.30, 0.70, 0.60, 0.50, 0.40, 0.30))
)
sim_boin_et_multi(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, scenarios = scenarios,
                  n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 1000,
                  seed = 123)

Selecting the OBD

At the end of a trial the DLT rates of the doses tried are made monotone by isotonic regression, and the response rates are estimated with one of three estimators (est_method): the observed rates (the default), the model-averaged unimodal isotonic regression of Lin and Yin (2017) ("multi_iso"), or the fractional polynomial logistic regression of Takeda et al. (2018) ("fp_logistic", which needs the ‘mfp’ package). The OBD is then chosen among the admissible doses with one of four rules (obd_method): the highest estimated response rate up to the estimated MTD ("max_resp", the default), or the highest value of one of the three utilities compared by Yamaguchi et al. (2024) ("utility_weighted", "utility_truncated_linear" and "utility_scoring").

boin_et_select_obd() selects the OBD from the final data of trials, so the same simulated trials can be judged under every rule.

oc_kept <- sim_boin_et(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true,
                       p_resp = p_resp, n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3,
                       n_trials = 2000, keep_trials = TRUE, seed = 123)
tr <- oc_kept$trials

select_percent <- function(est_method, obd_method) {
  obd <- boin_et_select_obd(n_pts = tr$n_pts, n_tox = tr$n_tox,
                            n_resp = tr$n_resp, target = 0.30,
                            target_resp = 0.60, est_method = est_method,
                            obd_method = obd_method,
                            early_stop = tr$early_stop)$obd
  as.numeric(table(factor(obd, levels = 1:6))) / length(obd) * 100
}

rules <- c("max_resp", "utility_weighted", "utility_truncated_linear",
           "utility_scoring")
selection <- rbind(
  t(sapply(rules, function(m) select_percent("observed", m))),
  "max_resp, multi_iso" = select_percent("multi_iso", "max_resp")
)
colnames(selection) <- paste0("DL", 1:6)
round(selection, 1)
#>                          DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5 DL6
#> max_resp                 1.5 16.1 47.1 26.7  7.0 0.5
#> utility_weighted         1.5 16.4 44.0 28.5  7.6 0.8
#> utility_truncated_linear 5.9 34.3 39.1 15.7  3.3 0.4
#> utility_scoring          2.1 16.8 39.4 29.6 10.1 1.0
#> max_resp, multi_iso      0.2 14.4 48.9 27.7  7.0 0.5

all.equal(unname(selection["max_resp", ]), unname(oc_kept$sel_percent))
#> [1] TRUE

The first row is the selection of sim_boin_et(), which calls boin_et_select_obd() with the same defaults. The fractional polynomial is fitted once for every distinct set of final data and takes longer:

sim_boin_et(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true,
            p_resp = p_resp, n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3,
            n_trials = 2000, est_method = "fp_logistic", seed = 123)

Dose moves that differ from ‘boinet’

After each cohort the admissibility of every dose is derived again from its data, and the trial stops early when no dose is admissible, or when the dose should be lowered and no admissible dose is found at or below the intended one. When the intended dose is not admissible, a stay or a de-escalation moves to the highest admissible dose below it, and an escalation to the lowest admissible dose above it, or stays when there is none.

Two rules differ from those of ‘boinet’ 1.6.0. Takeda et al. (2018) do not allow dose skipping during escalation, so a dose excluded by its DLT data also excludes every higher dose, as in the later BF-BOIN-ET design and the ‘bfboinet’ package, and an escalation from the highest dose ends the trial when that dose is excluded. In ‘boinet’, an escalation can skip a dose excluded by its DLT data and reach an untried higher dose, and an escalation from the highest dose stays there even when it is excluded. boinet_compatible = TRUE applies these rules of ‘boinet’ in every BOIN-ET and TITE-BOIN-ET function.

skip_design <- list(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60,
                    p_true = c(0.10, 0.20, 0.45, 0.50, 0.55),
                    p_resp = c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50, 0.60),
                    n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 2000,
                    seed = 123)
oc_default <- do.call(sim_boin_et, skip_design)
oc_boinet <- do.call(sim_boin_et,
                     c(skip_design, list(boinet_compatible = TRUE)))
round(rbind(default = oc_default$n_pts_dose,
            boinet = oc_boinet$n_pts_dose), 2)
#>          DL1   DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5
#> default 5.20 14.65 9.73 4.77 1.13
#> boinet  4.84 11.57 9.47 6.89 3.05

Doses 4 and 5, with DLT probabilities of 0.50 and 0.55, receive 5.9 patients per trial on average under the default rules and 9.9 under those of ‘boinet’, which let an escalation from dose 2 skip dose 3 once it is excluded.

TITE-BOIN-ET

When the DLT and the response take long to assess compared with the time between arrivals, TITE-BOIN-ET doses new patients while earlier ones are still assessed. A patient still under assessment counts in the DLT and response rates of a dose by the fraction of the window followed so far (Takeda et al., 2020), and the decision rule of BOIN-ET is applied to these rates. The admissibility of the doses counts such a patient as a patient without the event, as in ‘boinet’.

The first patient of a cohort arrives at the time of the previous decision, and the next decision is due when the next patient arrives. While fewer than a share min_completed_share of the patients at the current dose have finished both assessments, the decision waits for the next assessment to end. The default, 0.5, is the rule of boinet::tite.boinet(). The simulations of Takeda et al. (2020) did not wait (min_completed_share = 0), and the article recommends such a rule when the accrual is fast. By default the times to DLT and to response are Weibull, with late_fraction and resp_late_fraction of the events in the second half of each window, and they are linked by a Gaussian copula with correlation resp_cor.

The setting of Takeda et al. (2020) is a DLT window of 28 days, a response window of 56 days and one patient every 14 days; the unit of time is the day.

tite_design <- list(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true,
                    p_resp = p_resp, n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3,
                    window = 28, resp_window = 56, accrual_rate = 1 / 14,
                    n_trials = 1000, seed = 123)
oc_tite <- do.call(sim_tite_boin_et, tite_design)
oc_tite
#> TITE-BOIN-ET operating characteristics
#>   target DLT rate      : 0.3
#>   target response rate : 0.6
#>   trials               : 1000
#>   cohorts              : 12 of size 3
#>   max sample size      : 36
#>   lambda1 / lambda2    : 0.14 / 0.35
#>   eta1                 : 0.48
#>   OBD selection        : max_resp with observed response rates
#> 
#>                        DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5  DL6 Total / No OBD
#> True DLT rate (%)      5.0 15.0 25.0 30.0 35.0 40.0               
#> True response rate (%) 5.0 35.0 55.0 65.0 75.0 70.0               
#> OBD selected (%)       1.1 18.0 44.8 26.9  6.1  0.4            2.7
#> Patients treated       4.0  9.3 13.5  6.9  1.8  0.2           35.6
#> Patients with DLT      0.2  1.5  3.4  2.1  0.7  0.1            7.9
#> Patients with response 0.2  3.2  7.4  4.5  1.4  0.2           16.9
#> 
#> Trials stopped early: 2.7%
#> Average trial duration: 616.5

oc_tite_0 <- do.call(sim_tite_boin_et,
                     c(tite_design, list(min_completed_share = 0)))
round(rbind(
  "wait for half" = c(oc_tite$sel_percent, weeks = oc_tite$duration / 7),
  "no wait" = c(oc_tite_0$sel_percent, weeks = oc_tite_0$duration / 7)
), 1)
#>               DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4 DL5 DL6 weeks
#> wait for half 1.1 18.0 44.8 26.9 6.1 0.4  88.1
#> no wait       0.9 20.7 45.6 23.0 7.2 0.3  77.1

The trials last 88 weeks on average with the default rule and 77 weeks without waiting. The duration runs from the arrival of the first patient to the last decision, which is the end of both assessments of every patient when all cohorts are enrolled. The durations reported by Takeda et al. (2020) correspond to counting also the interval between arrivals before the first patient.

BF-BOIN-ET

In BF-BOIN-ET a cohort is treated at the current dose, and the next cohort starts with the first patient who arrives once the DLT outcomes of the cohort are known. The patients who arrive in between are backfilled one by one, when the current dose is not the lowest, to the lower dose with the highest utility among those with a promising response rate. The utility is defined by the scores psi00, psi_dlt_no_resp, psi_resp_no_dlt and psi11 of a patient without DLT or response, with a DLT only, with a response only and with both. The dose escalation uses the DLT rate at the current dose with the boundaries of BOIN, and stays after 1 DLT in 3 patients. A dose with n_elimination patients or more is excluded for good when its DLT or response data are poor, a dose excluded by its DLT data taking every higher dose with it. The OBD is the admissible dose up to the estimated MTD with the highest utility. The rules are those of bfboinet::get.oc.backboinet().

The example of ‘bfboinet’ has five doses, ten cohorts of three, windows of one month and three patients a month; the unit of time is the month.

bf_design <- list(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.25,
                  p_true = c(0.03, 0.05, 0.20, 0.22, 0.45),
                  p_resp = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.50, 0.68, 0.70),
                  n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3, window = 1,
                  accrual_rate = 3, n_trials = 1000, seed = 123)
oc_bf <- do.call(sim_bf_boin_et, bf_design)
oc_bf
#> BF-BOIN-ET operating characteristics
#>   target DLT rate      : 0.3
#>   target response rate : 0.25
#>   trials               : 1000
#>   cohorts              : 10 of size 3
#>   patients per dose    : 12 at most with backfill
#>   lambda1 / lambda2    : 0.2365 / 0.3585
#>   eta1                 : 0.1968
#> 
#>                        DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5 Total / No OBD
#> True DLT rate (%)      3.0  5.0 20.0 22.0 45.0               
#> True response rate (%) 5.0 10.0 50.0 68.0 70.0               
#> OBD selected (%)       2.2  3.5 41.0 47.8  5.4            0.1
#> Patients treated       4.1  5.9 11.3  9.7  5.2           36.1
#> Patients backfilled    0.7  1.3  4.5  2.7  0.2            9.4
#> Patients with DLT      0.1  0.3  2.3  2.1  2.4            7.2
#> Patients with response 0.2  0.6  5.6  6.6  3.7           16.6
#> 
#> Trials stopped early: 0%
#> Average trial duration: 16.8

With suspend = 0.33 the next cohort may start while a third of the patients at the current dose are still assessed for DLT, which is the BF-BOIN-ET-A design of Takeda et al. (2025); the default, suspend = 0, is their BF-BOIN-ET-C design.

oc_bf_a <- do.call(sim_bf_boin_et, c(bf_design, list(suspend = 0.33)))
round(rbind(
  "BF-BOIN-ET-C" = c(oc_bf$sel_percent, patients = oc_bf$total_n_pts,
                     backfilled = oc_bf$total_n_bf,
                     months = oc_bf$duration),
  "BF-BOIN-ET-A" = c(oc_bf_a$sel_percent, patients = oc_bf_a$total_n_pts,
                     backfilled = oc_bf_a$total_n_bf,
                     months = oc_bf_a$duration)
), 1)
#>              DL1 DL2  DL3  DL4 DL5 patients backfilled months
#> BF-BOIN-ET-C 2.2 3.5 41.0 47.8 5.4     36.1        9.4   16.8
#> BF-BOIN-ET-A 3.2 3.6 40.8 45.5 6.1     33.6        6.1   13.3

The patients include the backfilled ones. The trials last 16.8 months on average under BF-BOIN-ET-C and 13.3 months under BF-BOIN-ET-A.

BOIN-ETC

When two drugs are given together, the doses form a matrix, with the L levels of drug A in the rows and the M levels of drug B in the columns. BOIN-ETC (Kakizume et al., 2024) divides the matrix into subtrials along which the DLT rate increases and runs the rules of BOIN-ET in each of them, from its lowest combination. A subtrial ends when the combination chosen for the next cohort already has n_earlystop patients (6 by default, n_stop of the article), and that combination is the candidate of the subtrial. The first subtrial goes up drug A at the lowest level of drug B and then along the highest level of drug A, A1B1, A2B1, ..., ALB1, ALB2, ..., ALBM. The three versions then differ (subtrials):

  • BOIN-ETC1 ("etc1", the default) and BOIN-ETC2 ("etc2") run one subtrial per level of drug A, from level L - 1 down to level 1, over levels 2 to M of drug B; when the candidate of the first subtrial is at level l of drug A and level 1 of drug B, they start at level l - 1 of drug A. BOIN-ETC2 starts every subtrial at level 2 of drug B. BOIN-ETC1 starts it next to the candidate of the previous subtrial, and the article and its code differ there: the text and the figures start one level of drug B lower, diagonally below the candidate (etc1_start = "diagonal", the default), and the code of the authors at the same level of drug B, directly below it (etc1_start = "below"), in both cases at level 2 or above.
  • BOIN-ETC3 ("etc3") runs L-shaped subtrials: the subtrial j goes up level j + 1 of drug B to level L - j of drug A and then along that level of drug A to level M of drug B.

The names follow the figures, the tables and the code of the article; the text of its Section 2.2 describes BOIN-ETC2 and BOIN-ETC3 the other way round. A combination is excluded when the posterior probability that its DLT rate exceeds target is above cutoff_eli = 0.95, and with it the higher combinations of its subtrial; the subtrial ends when its lowest combination is excluded, and the trial ends when that combination is A1B1. In the code of the authors, the choice among the neighboring combinations when the decision of BOIN-ET is E/S/D moves one combination down when the combination below the current one is untreated; rule4 = "authors_code" applies this rule, and rule4 = "paper", the default, the rule of the text. Only etc1_start = "below" with rule4 = "authors_code" reproduces the allocation published for BOIN-ETC1.

At the end of the trial the DLT rates are made monotone along both drugs by bivariate isotonic regression, the MTD combination of every level of drug A bounds the candidates of that level, and the optimal dose combination (ODC) is the treated, not excluded candidate with the highest posterior mean of the utility of BOIN12, with the scores psi00 and psi11 (40 and 60 by default). boin_etc_select_obd() applies this selection to completed trials. When candidates tie, odc_tie = "lowest" (the default) selects the lowest one, and odc_tie = "all" counts every tied candidate, as the percentages of the article do.

Scenario 1 of the article has two levels of drug A, three of drug B, a target DLT rate of 0.30, a target response rate of 0.60 and at most 24 patients.

p_true_ab <- matrix(c(0.05, 0.10, 0.10, 0.30, 0.30, 0.50), nrow = 2)
p_resp_ab <- matrix(c(0.10, 0.25, 0.25, 0.60, 0.60, 0.65), nrow = 2)

oc_etc <- sim_boin_etc(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true_ab,
                       p_resp = p_resp_ab, n_cohort = 8, cohort_size = 3,
                       n_trials = 2000, seed = 123)
oc_etc
#> BOIN-ETC1 operating characteristics
#>   target DLT rate      : 0.3
#>   target response rate : 0.6
#>   dose levels          : 2 of drug A, 3 of drug B
#>   trials               : 2000
#>   cohorts              : 8 of size 3
#>   max sample size      : 24
#>   subtrial end (n_stop): 6
#>   lambda1/lambda2/eta1 : 0.14 / 0.35 / 0.48
#>   start of a row       : diagonal
#>   rule 4               : paper

The true ODCs, the combinations with the highest utility among those with a DLT rate at most 0.30, are A2B2, A1B3. The three versions, and BOIN-ETC1 with the rules of the code of the authors, compare as follows, with tied ODCs counted as in the article:

etc_versions <- list(
  "BOIN-ETC1" = list(subtrials = "etc1"),
  "BOIN-ETC1, code" = list(subtrials = "etc1", etc1_start = "below",
                           rule4 = "authors_code"),
  "BOIN-ETC2" = list(subtrials = "etc2"),
  "BOIN-ETC3" = list(subtrials = "etc3")
)
etc_runs <- lapply(etc_versions, function(v) {
  do.call(sim_boin_etc,
          c(list(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true_ab,
                 p_resp = p_resp_ab, n_cohort = 8, cohort_size = 3,
                 n_trials = 2000, odc_tie = "all", seed = 123), v))
})
round(t(sapply(etc_runs, function(o) {
  c("ODC selected (%)" = o$pct_true_obd_selected,
    "Patients at ODC (%)" = o$pct_patients_true_obd,
    "Patients" = o$total_n_pts, "Subtrials" = o$mean_subtrials)
})), 1)
#>                 ODC selected (%) Patients at ODC (%) Patients Subtrials
#> BOIN-ETC1                   73.4                42.1     22.3         2
#> BOIN-ETC1, code             75.1                42.7     22.3         2
#> BOIN-ETC2                   73.4                42.1     22.3         2
#> BOIN-ETC3                   73.4                42.1     22.3         2

gBOIN-ET

gBOIN-ET (Takeda, Morita and Taguri, 2022) is BOIN-ET for graded outcomes, as gBOIN is BOIN for toxicity grades (vignette("simFastBOIN-introduction")). Every category of the toxicity and of the efficacy carries a score, here the equivalent toxicity score of the article (0 for grades 0 and 1, 0.5, 1 and 1.5 for grades 2, 3 and 4) and its equivalent efficacy score (0 for stable or progressive disease, 1 for a partial and 1.5 for a complete response). The scores are divided by their maximum, and the mean scores of the patients at the current dose take the place of the DLT and response rates in the rules of BOIN-ET; the admissibility of a dose uses the posterior distributions of the mean scores given their totals. The targets are on the same scale, 0.47 / 1.5 and 0.95 / 1.5 for an equivalent toxicity score of 0.47 and an equivalent efficacy score of 0.95.

The true probabilities form two matrices, with one row per category and one column per dose. Scenario 1 of the article has six doses and 30 patients in cohorts of three; the efficacy is given by the probabilities of a complete and of a partial response.

p_grade <- rbind(
  "Grade 0-1" = c(0.83, 0.75, 0.62, 0.51, 0.34, 0.19),
  "Grade 2" = c(0.12, 0.15, 0.18, 0.19, 0.16, 0.11),
  "Grade 3" = c(0.04, 0.07, 0.11, 0.14, 0.15, 0.11),
  "Grade 4" = c(0.01, 0.03, 0.09, 0.16, 0.35, 0.59)
)
cr <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.50, 0.55, 0.60)
pr <- c(0.05, 0.20, 0.35, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20)
p_resp_grade <- rbind("SD or PD" = 1 - cr - pr, PR = pr, CR = cr)

g_design <- list(target = 0.47 / 1.5, target_resp = 0.95 / 1.5,
                 p_grade = p_grade, p_resp_grade = p_resp_grade,
                 score = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5), score_resp = c(0, 1, 1.5),
                 n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 2000,
                 seed = 123)
oc_g <- do.call(sim_gboin_et, g_design)
oc_g
#> gBOIN-ET operating characteristics
#>   target toxicity score: 0.3133333
#>   target efficacy score: 0.6333333
#>   trials               : 2000
#>   cohorts              : 10 of size 3
#>   max sample size      : 30
#>   lambda1 / lambda2    : 0.1413 / 0.3733
#>   eta1                 : 0.5
#>   OBD selection        : max_resp with observed efficacy scores
#> 
#>                         DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5  DL6 Total / No OBD
#> True toxicity score (%) 7.7 12.7 22.3 31.7 50.3 70.0               
#> True efficacy score (%) 8.3 23.3 38.3 63.3 68.3 73.3               
#> OBD selected (%)        2.2  9.6 30.2 54.9  2.9  0.0            0.1
#> Patients treated        3.4  5.4  9.3 10.6  1.3  0.1           30.0
#> Toxicity score          0.2  0.7  2.1  3.3  0.7  0.0            7.0
#> Efficacy score          0.3  1.3  3.5  6.7  0.9  0.1           12.7
#> 
#> Trials stopped early: 0.1%

The boundaries for these targets, 0.14, 0.37 and 0.5, are those printed in the article. The article selects the optimal dose from the efficacy scores estimated by a linear fractional polynomial (est_method = "fp_linear"), and its program does so among the doses with at least six patients (min_obd_sample = 6). The same trials give

oc_g_article <- do.call(sim_gboin_et,
                        c(g_design, list(est_method = "fp_linear",
                                         min_obd_sample = 6)))
round(rbind(
  default = c(oc_g$sel_percent, "No OBD" = oc_g$percent_no_obd),
  article = c(oc_g_article$sel_percent,
              "No OBD" = oc_g_article$percent_no_obd)
), 1)
#>         DL1 DL2  DL3  DL4 DL5 DL6 No OBD
#> default 2.2 9.6 30.2 54.9 2.9   0    0.1
#> article 0.5 4.7 35.2 55.1 3.0   0    1.4

The SAS program of the authors does not draw the categories from the probabilities that the article tabulates: it draws one Bernoulli variate for every category and takes the highest category that comes up, so that the lower categories are rarer than tabulated. The results above are therefore not those of Table 1 of the article; inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2022.R simulates the probabilities that the program draws. The toxicity and the efficacy of a patient are linked as in BOIN-ET, by a Gaussian copula with correlation resp_cor, and with two categories scored 0 and 1 for both outcomes the trials are those of sim_boin_et() for the same seed.

TITE-gBOIN-ET

TITE-gBOIN-ET (Takeda, Yamaguchi, Taguri and Morita, 2023) applies the rules of gBOIN-ET at the decision times of TITE-BOIN-ET: the next cohort is enrolled while earlier patients are still assessed, and the mean score of a dose divides the scores observed so far by the effective number of patients, in which a patient still under assessment counts by the fraction of the window followed so far. The decision waits while fewer than min_completed_share of the patients at the current dose have finished both assessments, and the admissibility counts a patient still under assessment as a patient without an event. These are the rules of boinet::tite.gboinet(), with the changes from ‘boinet’ described above.

Scenario 3 of the article has the toxicity of the example above and four efficacy categories, progressive disease, stable disease, partial and complete response, scored 0, 0.25, 1 and 3, with a target efficacy score of 1.75. The trials have 36 patients in cohorts of three, a toxicity window of 30 days, an efficacy window of 60 days and one patient every 10 days on average; the unit of time is the day.

p_resp_grade_4 <- rbind(
  PD = c(0.60, 0.50, 0.30, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05),
  SD = c(0.30, 0.20, 0.20, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15),
  PR = c(0.05, 0.20, 0.35, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20),
  CR = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.50, 0.55, 0.60)
)
tg_design <- list(target = 0.47 / 1.5, target_resp = 1.75 / 3,
                  p_grade = p_grade, p_resp_grade = p_resp_grade_4,
                  score = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5), score_resp = c(0, 0.25, 1, 3),
                  n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3, window = 30,
                  resp_window = 60, accrual_rate = 1 / 10, n_trials = 1000,
                  seed = 123)
oc_tg <- do.call(sim_tite_gboin_et, tg_design)
oc_tg
#> TITE-gBOIN-ET operating characteristics
#>   target toxicity score: 0.3133333
#>   target efficacy score: 0.5833333
#>   trials               : 1000
#>   cohorts              : 12 of size 3
#>   max sample size      : 36
#>   lambda1 / lambda2    : 0.1413 / 0.3733
#>   eta1                 : 0.46
#>   OBD selection        : max_resp with observed efficacy scores
#> 
#>                         DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5  DL6 Total / No OBD
#> True toxicity score (%) 7.7 12.7 22.3 31.7 50.3 70.0               
#> True efficacy score (%) 9.2 18.3 28.3 57.9 62.9 67.9               
#> OBD selected (%)        4.3  7.2 22.3 60.8  5.0  0.2            0.2
#> Patients treated        3.5  5.6  9.2 14.2  3.2  0.3           36.0
#> Toxicity score          0.3  0.7  2.1  4.5  1.6  0.2            9.4
#> Efficacy score          0.3  1.0  2.6  8.2  2.0  0.2           14.4
#> 
#> Trials stopped early: 0.2%
#> Average trial duration: 518.2

oc_tg_wait <- do.call(sim_tite_gboin_et,
                      c(tg_design, list(min_completed_share = 1)))
round(rbind(
  "wait for half" = c(oc_tg$sel_percent, weeks = oc_tg$duration / 7),
  "wait for all" = c(oc_tg_wait$sel_percent,
                     weeks = oc_tg_wait$duration / 7)
), 1)
#>               DL1 DL2  DL3  DL4 DL5 DL6 weeks
#> wait for half 4.3 7.2 22.3 60.8 5.0 0.2  74.0
#> wait for all  3.3 8.0 21.3 63.7 3.5 0.1 117.5

The trials last 74 weeks on average when the decision waits for half of the patients at the current dose, the default of the article and of ‘boinet’, and 118 weeks when it waits for all of them. The article excludes a dose for its efficacy with a cutoff of 0.95 (cutoff_eli_resp = 0.95); the default, 0.99, is that of the other functions of the family and of ‘boinet’. The R program of the supporting information of the article differs from these rules in two points, which inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2023.R describes: when one dose has the highest mean efficacy score among the current dose and its neighbors, it can move to any lower dose at random, and it excludes doses with the effective numbers of patients.

How the implementation is checked

The scripts in inst/reproduce/ and inst/validation/ compare the package with the articles and with the packages and the code of the authors, and write the tables of judgments in their results/ folders, which are summarized here. A simulated cell passes when it lies within four standard errors of the difference between the two simulations plus the rounding of the published value.

  • Takeda et al. (2018). 68 of the 68 entries of the boundaries and of the decisions of Table 2 agree exactly. Of the 156 cells of Table 3, 142 pass; 10 of the 14 others are in scenario 11, where the printed response rate of 0.55 at the lowest dose does not fit the published results, and ‘boinet’ too selects that dose far more often than the article reports.
  • Takeda et al. (2020). Of the 324 cells of Table 2, 295 pass. The BOIN-ET rows fail in 12 cells, in scenario 11 and in the cells that also fail for Table 3 of the 2018 article. Of the 17 cells of TITE-BOIN-ET that fail, 8 are in scenario 11 and 6 are early terminations, durations and allocations in scenarios 8, 9, 10 and 12, which agree better with an exclusion of doses that uses only the patients whose outcomes are known; the article does not say which patients this rule uses, and the package keeps the rule of ‘boinet’. The remaining 3 are not explained. The durations are compared after adding the mean interval between arrivals before the first patient.
  • Takeda et al. (2025). 336 of the 336 cells of Tables 1 and 2 pass, with and without the suspension rule.
  • ‘boinet’. The operating characteristics of sim_boin_et() and sim_tite_boin_et() with boinet_compatible = TRUE are compared with those of boinet::boinet() and boinet::tite.boinet(): 312 of 312 cells pass for BOIN-ET and 196 of 196 for TITE-BOIN-ET. The packages draw their random numbers differently, so they agree in distribution, not trial by trial. The tests also compare the boundaries with boinet::gridoptim() and the OBD of simulated trials with boinet::obd.select(): the same dose is selected in every trial, except that doses whose utilities are equal as fractions tie here, where rounding error decides between them in ‘boinet’.
  • ‘bfboinet’. 85 of the 85 cells comparing sim_bf_boin_et() with bfboinet::get.oc.backboinet() pass.
  • Kakizume et al. (2024). With etc1_start = "below" and rule4 = "authors_code" for BOIN-ETC1, 1168 of the 1176 values of the allocation (the mean numbers of patients at every combination of Supplementary Tables S4 and S5, and %nODC and #N of Table 3 and Supplementary Tables S1 and S6 to S9) pass, and the 8 others are misprints that disagree with the other tables of the article. The 996 values of the selection (%ODC and Supplementary Tables S2 and S3) are listed for information, because the code of the authors estimates the DLT rates with Iso::biviso(), whose convergence errors decide between the combinations that tie for the MTD combination of a level of drug A in the exact isotonic regression of the package; 982 of them lie within the tolerance.
  • The code of the authors. inst/validation/compare-with-BOINETC.R runs the R code of the authors. With the random numbers of R after set.seed(1234) it gives 1657 of the 1692 published values of the allocation and the selection of Scenarios 1 to 5 and 7 to 9 to the printed digits, and the 35 others are misprints. On the same trials, boin_etc_select_obd() selects other combinations than the code in 4.6 percent of the trials on average, because combinations tie for the MTD combination of a level of drug A in the exact isotonic regression or because the code selects an untreated or excluded combination; no trial differs for another reason.
  • Takeda et al. (2022). 12 of the 12 boundaries printed in the article for gBOIN-ET and BOIN-ET are reproduced to the printed digits. The cells of Table 1 are simulated with the probabilities that the SAS program of the authors draws, the printed boundaries, the linear fractional polynomial, min_obd_sample = 6, independent outcomes and boinet_compatible = TRUE, the rules closest to that program: 119 of the 130 cells pass, 4 are explained by rules of the program that the package does not have, which a transcription of the program in Python reproduces, and 7 fail, 6 of them numbers of patients, for a reason that was not found.
  • Takeda et al. (2023). 3 of the 3 boundaries printed in the article are reproduced. The R program of its supporting information, written again in C++ with the random numbers of R, reproduces the summaries that the supporting information holds for the program exactly. It differs from the article and from ‘boinet’ in the two points described above. With the rules of ‘boinet’, the printed boundaries, independent outcomes and the efficacy cutoff of the article, 273 of the 570 cells of Table 1 and of Tables S2 to S6 pass and the 297 others are explained by these two points: against the program without them, 570 of the 570 cells pass.
  • ‘boinet’ for gBOIN-ET and TITE-gBOIN-ET. With boinet_compatible = TRUE, 156 of the 156 values comparing sim_gboin_et() with boinet::gboinet() and 168 of the 168 comparing sim_tite_gboin_et() with boinet::tite.gboinet() pass, in 6 and 6 scenarios of the two articles, under the four selection rules.
  • Separate implementations. The trials of the six engines agree exactly, trial by trial, with implementations written in Python, from the R code of ‘boinet’ and ‘bfboinet’ and, for BOIN-ETC, gBOIN-ET and TITE-gBOIN-ET, from the rules described above, and fed with the same random numbers; so does the selection of BOIN-ETC. With two categories scored 0 and 1, the trials of gBOIN-ET and TITE-gBOIN-ET are those of BOIN-ET and TITE-BOIN-ET.
